idiom_name: Connection::open + prepared INSERT with params!, writer thread owning the connection
implementation_notes: rusqlite gives a safe, blocking SQLite binding: Connection::open creates the file, pragma_update sets journal_mode and synchronous once, Connection::prepare builds the append statement, and params! maps the record's fields into bound values; the classic Store and interceptor roles collapse into a struct plus a writer loop. The connection is not Sync, which the type system makes useful: either wrap it in a Mutex<Connection> for a small store, or - better - move it into a dedicated thread fed by an mpsc channel, so the single-writer invariant is expressed by ownership instead of by discipline. Payloads are serde-serialised JSON or typed columns, and retention is a DELETE by timestamp plus VACUUM. Choose this variant for an embedded, synchronous store; choose the sqlx variant when the service is already async and the store is a shared database.
pitfalls: A Mutex<Connection> serialises reporting behind the writer; WAL plus a second read-only connection (OpenFlags::SQLITE_OPEN_READ_ONLY) keeps audit queries off the tap's path.
rusqlite is blocking: calling it from an async task stalls the executor, so the writer belongs on its own thread or inside spawn_blocking.
serde_json rendering changes when fields are renamed or made optional; version the stored payload type or store an explicit serde_json::Value so history stays readable.
A dropped Receiver (writer thread exited) turns every send into a silent Err; count it, or the store stops recording without any error on the delivery path.

variants.name: sqlx async pool store with a spawned writer task
variants.idiom_name: SqlitePool + spawn'ed writer task fed by tokio mpsc
variants.implementation_notes: When the service is already async, sqlx keeps the store on the same runtime: SqlitePool multiplexes a small pool of connections, a prepared query (sqlx::query or the compile-time checked query! macro) performs the append, and migrations are managed with sqlx::migrate!. The audit copy runs on a spawned task fed by tokio::sync::mpsc, so the request path only offers the record (try_send) and a slow store becomes a drop counter rather than a latency spike, which is what replaces the classic interceptor. Retention is a scheduled DELETE by timestamp. Choose it over rusqlite when the application is tokio-based and the store is shared; prefer the embedded variant when the audit log is a local file and dependency weight matters.
pitfalls: SQLite still allows only one writer: a large pool turns concurrent writes into SQLITE_BUSY, so size the pool for readers and serialise the tap (one writer task) or accept the retries.
sqlx::query! checks SQL against the schema at build time and therefore needs DATABASE_URL or a cached offline metadata file; without it the build breaks in CI.
A dropped Sender/Receiver ends the writer task silently; monitor it, because nothing on the delivery path will report that auditing stopped.
Backups must include the -wal and -shm files (or use VACUUM INTO); restoring only the main database file loses the tail of the audit log.
